items.sentence: My sister work in a hospital near the station.
items.gold_full: My sister works in a hospital near the station.
items.why_en: With he/she/it in the present simple, the verb takes -s.

items.sentence: I am engineer at a small software company.
items.gold_full: I am an engineer at a small software company.
items.why_en: English needs a/an before a job after 'be'.

items.sentence: I have seen that film last week with my brother.
items.gold_full: I saw that film last week with my brother.
items.why_en: With a finished time like 'last week', use the past simple, not the present perfect.

items.sentence: I live in London since 2019.
items.gold_full: I have lived in London since 2019.
items.why_en: For something that started in the past and continues, 'since' needs the present perfect.

items.sentence: Can you give me some informations about the course?
items.gold_full: Can you give me some information about the course?
items.why_en: 'Information' is uncountable and has no plural.

items.sentence: I am agree with you about the price.
items.gold_full: I agree with you about the price.
items.why_en: 'Agree' is a verb, so no 'am' before it.

items.sentence: It depends of the weather tomorrow.
items.gold_full: It depends on the weather tomorrow.
items.why_en: The verb is 'depend on', not 'depend of'.

items.sentence: Where you live now?
items.gold_full: Where do you live now?
items.why_en: Questions in the present simple need 'do/does' before the subject.

items.sentence: I am looking forward to see you on Friday.
items.gold_full: I am looking forward to seeing you on Friday.
items.why_en: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.

items.sentence: My skin is very sensible to the sun.
items.gold_full: My skin is very sensitive to the sun.
items.why_en: 'Sensible' means reasonable; for reacting easily, the word is 'sensitive'.

items.sentence: I didn't went to work yesterday because I was sick.
items.gold_full: I didn't go to work yesterday because I was sick.
items.why_en: After 'didn't', the verb stays in the base form.

items.sentence: This phone is more cheaper than my old one.
items.gold_full: This phone is cheaper than my old one.
items.why_en: Short adjectives take -er alone; 'more' is not added.

items.sentence: I need to make my homework before dinner.
items.gold_full: I need to do my homework before dinner.
items.why_en: English says 'do homework', not 'make homework'.

items.sentence: We stayed there for three night.
items.gold_full: We stayed there for three nights.
items.why_en: After a number above one, the noun is plural.

items.sentence: There were much people at the concert.
items.gold_full: There were many people at the concert.
items.why_en: 'People' is countable, so it takes 'many', not 'much'.

items.sentence: If I will have time, I will call you.
items.gold_full: If I have time, I will call you.
items.why_en: In a first conditional, the if-clause uses the present, not 'will'.

items.sentence: He said me that the meeting was cancelled.
items.gold_full: He told me that the meeting was cancelled.
items.why_en: 'Say' takes no person directly; use 'tell me' (or 'said to me').

items.sentence: The man which lives next door is a pilot.
items.gold_full: The man who lives next door is a pilot.
items.why_en: For people, the relative pronoun is 'who' (or 'that'), not 'which'.

items.sentence: We discussed about the new project for an hour.
items.gold_full: We discussed the new project for an hour.
items.why_en: 'Discuss' takes a direct object, with no 'about'.

items.sentence: I love the nature, so I go hiking every weekend.
items.gold_full: I love nature, so I go hiking every weekend.
items.why_en: When 'nature' means nature in general, it has no 'the'.

items.sentence: I wish I can speak French better.
items.gold_full: I wish I could speak French better.
items.why_en: After 'wish' about the present, the verb moves back: 'could', not 'can'.

items.sentence: I have worked here since three years.
items.gold_full: I have worked here for three years.
items.why_en: 'For' goes with a length of time; 'since' goes with a starting point.

items.sentence: They bought a red big car last month.
items.gold_full: They bought a big red car last month.
items.why_en: Size comes before colour in English adjective order.

items.sentence: I like very much this song.
items.error_type: word order (adverb between verb and object)
items.gold_full: I like this song very much.
items.why_en: English does not put 'very much' between the verb and its object.

items.sentence: We have a meeting in Monday morning.
items.gold_full: We have a meeting on Monday morning.
items.why_en: Days, including 'Monday morning', take 'on'.

items.sentence: She is married with a doctor from Canada.
items.gold_full: She is married to a doctor from Canada.
items.why_en: In English, you are 'married to' someone.

items.sentence: Can you control the report before I send it?
items.gold_full: Can you check the report before I send it?
items.why_en: 'Control' means direct or limit; looking for mistakes is 'check'.

items.sentence: I go to the gym every days after work.
items.gold_full: I go to the gym every day after work.
items.why_en: 'Every' is followed by a singular noun.

items.sentence: Who did you go to the cinema with?
items.note: Preposition at the end is normal English; 'With whom' would be overly formal.

items.sentence: Everyone brought their own lunch to the picnic.
I just ate, so I'm not hungry right now.
items.note: American English uses past simple with 'just'; do not force 'I've just eaten'.

items.sentence: If I were you, I'd take the earlier train.
We've got two kids and a dog.
items.note: 'Have got' and 'kids' are informal but correct.

items.sentence: My flight got cancelled, so I stayed another night in Rome.
items.note: 'Got cancelled' (get-passive) and the British spelling 'cancelled' are both correct.

items.sentence: Can I get a coffee to go, please?
items.note: Informal but standard way to order.

items.sentence: Hopefully the weather will be better tomorrow.
It's the first time I've been to Japan.
What are you up to this weekend?
She's been working there for about five years.
I didn't do much this weekend, just relaxed at home.
items.note: Casual ellipsis after the comma is fine in chat.
